parsed.summary: The writer goes by coach to Sir Ph. Warwicke's, where the streets are full of footballs during a great frost, and finds him walking with Mr. Coventry in St. James's Park. He then calls on Lord of Oxford for consent about felling the King's timber, which the Lord Privy Seal holds up. After news at the Coffee-house that the Dutch have taken some colliers, he spends the day at the office, at dinner, and at Sir W. Batten's, where the light-house patent is mentioned. He returns to the office, goes home to supper and bed, and sits up playing cards with his wife until past two.

parsed.summary: Pepys wakes angry at his boy for lying in bed and forgetting his lute, then spends the morning at his office and the day at business. After dinner at Gresham College he finds Commissioner Pett remarkably able in discussing Castle's ship draught, and he takes great pleasure in hearing them talk. That evening a letter from Plymouth reports two of the navy's ships lost aground in the Straits, three more nearly lost, and a Dutch fleet heading there, which he calls most sad news. Returning home, he is much troubled to learn that his canary bird of three or four years is dead.

canon.summary: Pepys went early to Mr. Povy, hoping to end his trouble of mind over the Tangier business, and offered Povy his treasurership back on Povy's own terms. Povy refused, and Pepys was briefly satisfied. Speaking with Creed afterwards, he was put in doubt that Povy would have to be reinstated, and he accepted the auditors' reasons as too plain to withstand. He then secured an order for Povy's payment of the remaining accounts to him, which he hoped would stop the thing being fastened upon him. In the morning he had heard that the fleets were engaged and that Captain Teddiman's legs were shot off in the Royall Katherine, but before night he learned that all were well and the ship had reached the fleet, which made him heartily glad.

parsed.subject: Mr. Povy
parsed.summary: The diarist sent his wife to Whitehall Chapel by Mr. Povy's coach on the Lord's day, and spent the morning drinking at the Harp and Ball, where he talked with the house's maid. At the chapel he heard the young Stillingfleete preach a plain, honest, grave sermon on the words "Fear the Lord in truth with all your heart," which he said was the most unconcerned and substantial preaching he had ever heard. Afterwards at Mr. Povy's house, the diarist found Povy's over-praise of everything nauseous, and his wife was not pleased by the diarist's large praise of the house. That evening, with friends at his own house, there was good music and an argument with Captain Taylor over a corant, which vexed Taylor but ended with all parting friends.

canon.summary: On the Lord's day, Mr. Povy's coach took the diarist and his wife to Whitehall Chapel, where he heard the young Stillingfleete preach on Samuel's words to the people. At Mr. Povy's dinner, Povy's excessive commending of his house made it nauseous to the diarist and was not well received by his wife. In the afternoon the diarist and Creed took a coach ride in the fields beyond St. Pancras in rain, then returned home to good music and guests. At supper an argument with Captain Taylor over a corant grew until the diarist vexed him, though all parted friends.

parsed.harm: head akeing with too much thoughts
parsed.summary: The writer lay long in bed with a head aching from too many thoughts. He was troubled that he had heard nothing said or done by my Lord Sandwich, until a Mr. Moore told him the King had said Sandwich had done nobly and worthily. Lifted by joy at the recent news of victory over the Dutch, he bought a coloured silk suit despite long resolving to wear only black. That evening, a supper with guests took the place of his stone-feast, and he ended the day glad it was over.

He read a play on the way to Brainford, where Mr. Povy's coach waited and Povy joined him for a merry trip to Sir R. Viner's pleasant house at Swakely. Viner showed them the house and grounds, including a black boy dried in an oven and kept in a box, and they dined and heard songs from Mrs. Worship in the long gallery. After concluding business about getting a promise of money, they returned by water and reached Woolwich about one in the morning.

parsed.summary: Pepys went to the office full of resolve to spend the day on business, and agreed to have Poynter act as his clerk for the victualling business. He spent the whole day alone in his little closet drawing up instructions for the Surveyors of the Ports that Sir W. Coventry had long wanted. At night a long discourse with Gibson showed him how little he understood of the victualling business and pursers' trade, leaving him ashamed and distrustful of the day's work, so he set it aside to think afresh in the morning. He then went home as promised to his wife for merriment, where neighbours danced and the company stayed merry below until two or three in the morning.

parsed.subject: my accounts
parsed.summary: The diarist rose early and spent the morning with Lord Bruncker and others on new instructions for signing and paying bills. At noon Mr. Hill and Mr. Houbland joined him, and he dined with them at the Beare, leaving his Lord's company to do so. After Mr. Andrews agreed to tallys for Tangier victualls, he cleared £210, but his mind was burdened by the accounts he had not yet reckoned. That evening he watched Lord Bruncker open and repair his watch, then felt vexed by Madam Williams' snappish answer, and he ended by hoping the frosty weather would lessen the plague while fearing it would continue into the next year.

canon.subject: my accounts
canon.summary: The diarist rose early and spent the morning with Lord Bruncker and others on new instructions for signing and paying bills. At noon Mr. Hill and Mr. Houbland joined him, and he dined with them at the Beare, leaving his Lord's company to do so. After Mr. Andrews agreed to tallys for Tangier victualls, he cleared £210, but his mind was burdened by the accounts he had not yet reckoned. That evening he watched Lord Bruncker open and repair his watch, then felt vexed by Madam Williams' snappish answer, and he ended by hoping the frosty weather would lessen the plague while fearing it would continue into the next year.
